transcript:
Your app just got featured on Product Hunt. 4,000 signups in the last 48 hours. By day seven, though, 90% of them were gone. So your signup page is converting, but your product isn't. Somewhere between account creation and the moment your app is supposed to become indispensable, 3,640 people decide it was not worth opening again. So you do not have a marketing problem. You do not even have a traffic problem. You have an onboarding architecture that never gave them a reason to come back after the first time. So your AI built the signup flow. It never built a reason to stay. Here's what we're going to do. Step one, a time to value target measured in seconds, not days. The user should experience the core value of your product within 60 seconds of sign up. Not watch a tour, not read documentation, but do the thing. If your app is a project tracker, they should have a project with tasks in it before the onboarding is finished.

So direct your AI to implement a guided first run experience that delivers the core action within 60 seconds using pre-filled templates or smart defaults. That's a win. Step two, progressive disclosure that gates complexity behind achievements. So do not show every feature on the first session. Unlock capabilities as the user demonstrates readiness. So first session, core workflow. Second session, customization. Third session, all the integrations. So direct your AI to implement a progressive disclosure system that tracks user milestones and reveals features incrementally based on their usage. That's going to work. And step three, a day one and day seven re-engagement trigger tied to something the user created. Not a generic come back please email. A notification about the thing that they built. Your project has three tasks due tomorrow. That's a reason to open the app. It's personal, right? So direct your AI to implement event-based re-engagement that references the user's own data.

Triggered at day one and day seven post sign-up. So your sign-up, it's converting. Now it's time to make that product convert.

claims.topic: User onboarding architecture, activation, and early retention for a newly acquired SaaS/product app
claims.problem: The transcript frames a scenario where the signup page converts well after a traffic spike, but most new users do not return by day seven. The asserted engineering problem is that the product's onboarding architecture fails to deliver immediate core value and a reason to come back after the first session, rather than a marketing or traffic deficiency.
technicalClaims: Claim: In the described scenario, high signup volume followed by roughly 90% day-seven abandonment indicates an activation and onboarding failure rather than a signup conversion, marketing, or traffic problem.

Claim: New users should experience the product's core value within about 60 seconds of signup; onboarding that mainly shows tours or documentation is treated as insufficient because it delays the user from performing the core action.

Claim: A guided first-run experience using pre-filled templates or smart defaults can shorten time to value by causing the user to complete or receive the product's core artifact/workflow before onboarding ends, such as a project tracker creating a project with tasks already in it.

Claim: Showing every feature in the first session is presented as harmful or ineffective; progressive disclosure that tracks milestones and reveals capabilities incrementally is claimed to match feature complexity to demonstrated user readiness across sessions.

Claim: Day-one and day-seven re-engagement should be event-based and reference data the user created, because a notification about the user's own artifact is claimed to provide a more personal and concrete reason to reopen the app than a generic comeback email.
claims.recommendedSolution: As a hypothesis for later validation, implement three onboarding/retention mechanisms: a guided first-run flow that delivers the core user action within 60 seconds of signup using pre-filled templates or smart defaults; a progressive disclosure system that tracks user milestones and unlocks or reveals features incrementally based on usage; and event-based re-engagement triggers at day one and day seven after signup that reference the user's own created data rather than sending generic reminders.
reasoning: The transcript's causal model is that signup conversion only proves users are willing to try the product; it does not prove they have experienced enough value to return.

If onboarding delays the core action through tours, documentation, empty states, or manual setup, users may leave before understanding why the product matters; reducing time to value to seconds is presented as the mechanism for improving activation.
Pre-filled templates and smart defaults are proposed to remove setup friction and ensure the user has a meaningful starting artifact or completed workflow during the first run.

Progressive disclosure is proposed to reduce first-session complexity by limiting the initial experience to the core workflow, then exposing customization and integrations only after usage milestones indicate readiness.
Event-based re-engagement is proposed to change notifications from generic marketing messages into context-specific prompts tied to user-owned data, making the reason to return concrete and personal.

The expected outcome is that the product itself begins converting signups into active users by creating immediate value, reducing early overwhelm, and giving users specific reasons to reopen the app after signup.
assumptions: The product has a clearly identifiable core action or core value moment that can be delivered shortly after signup.
The core value moment can realistically occur within approximately 60 seconds without requiring lengthy external integrations, manual data entry, compliance checks, or human approval.
The application can safely generate useful pre-filled templates, demo content, smart defaults, or initial user-specific artifacts without misleading the user or polluting real data.
User milestones and achievements can be instrumented in a way that reliably represents readiness for additional features.
The product has or can add a feature-gating or feature-reveal mechanism without breaking discoverability for users who already know what they need.
The app has permission and delivery channels for day-one and day-seven notifications, such as email, push, or in-app messaging.
The user will have created or received meaningful data during onboarding that can be referenced later in a personalized re-engagement trigger.

Early churn in the described scenario is materially influenced by onboarding and activation design, not solely by unrelated factors such as poor product-market fit, pricing, bugs, performance, missing core functionality, or low-intent traffic from Product Hunt.

implications.detail: The product may need explicit onboarding state, milestone tracking, feature-visibility rules, and event-triggered messaging rather than treating signup as the end of the acquisition flow.
The implementation requires developers or AI coding tools to encode the product's core action, default content, and readiness milestones clearly enough that onboarding can be tested against them.
Day-one and day-seven triggers require scheduled or event-driven job execution and monitoring so re-engagement messages fire at the intended times.
Progressive disclosure adds conditional feature exposure logic that must stay aligned with product changes, new features, and updated onboarding milestones.
If personalized re-engagement depends on user-created data, notification generation must handle missing, deleted, incomplete, or stale artifacts gracefully.

uncertainties: Repository inspection can verify whether a guided first-run flow exists, whether it attempts to create or pre-fill a core artifact, and whether tours/documentation are the primary onboarding mechanism.

Repository inspection can verify whether there is instrumentation for signup time, onboarding completion, core action completion, user milestones, and feature reveal state, but it cannot by itself prove that users experience core value within 60 seconds in production.
Repository inspection can verify whether feature visibility is milestone-based or session-based, but runtime analytics are needed to determine whether this reduces abandonment or improves activation.

Repository inspection can verify whether day-one and day-seven scheduled triggers exist and whether message templates reference user data, but production delivery logs and engagement metrics are needed to determine whether users receive and respond to them.

The transcript does not define the specific product, its core action, current onboarding implementation, analytics stack, notification channel, or baseline retention metrics beyond the illustrative 4,000 signups and 90% day-seven loss scenario.

The claimed 60-second target and day-one/day-seven cadence are asserted as prescriptions, but the transcript does not provide empirical evidence that those thresholds are optimal for every product category.

The transcript does not address tradeoffs such as user consent for notifications, privacy constraints around referencing user data, the risk of creating unwanted demo content, or cases where exposing integrations early is necessary for the product's core value.

onboardingPrompt:
You are a read-only repository investigation agent. Do not edit files, create branches, run migrations, generate implementation code, or refactor anything. Your task is to map the current architecture relevant to user onboarding, activation, and early retention for this SaaS/product application before any later audit evaluates proposed changes.

Important: do not assume there is an onboarding problem. Do not evaluate or recommend a solution yet. Build an evidence-backed briefing of how the repository currently handles the new-user lifecycle from account creation through first meaningful product use and early return paths.

Scope your discovery to repository evidence only. You may inspect code, configs, tests, schemas, migrations, routes, jobs, analytics definitions, templates, infrastructure manifests, docs, and observability setup. If you run read-only commands, report what you ran. Do not rely on product intuition without file-level support.

Map the current system in these areas:

1. Product and runtime boundaries
- Identify the app type, major services/packages, frontend/backend boundaries, API style, authentication/session model, persistence layer, job/queue/scheduler system, notification providers, analytics/telemetry stack, and deployment/configuration conventions.
- Note ownership/module boundaries that matter for signup, onboarding, first-run product use, feature visibility, and lifecycle messaging.

2. Signup and post-signup control flow
- Trace the new-user path from public signup or invite acceptance through account/user/org creation, initial redirect, first authenticated screen, and any onboarding or setup screens.
- Provide exact routes, controllers/actions, components, hooks, services, events, tables/schemas, and tests involved.
- Identify branching by plan, role, organization/workspace creation, invitation, authentication provider, trial state, feature flags, or environment.

3. First-session product experience
- Determine what the app appears to define as its central product workflow or core artifact, if discoverable from code and tests. Keep this as a confirmed fact only when supported by routes, naming, domain models, analytics events, docs, or tests; otherwise mark as inference or unknown.
- Document whether first-run screens focus on setup, data entry, empty states, guided actions, documentation links, tours, sample/demo/default content, import/integration steps, or immediate creation/use of domain objects. Do not judge adequacy yet.
- Capture required dependencies before a new user can reach meaningful product functionality, such as external integrations, billing, approvals, workspace membership, data import, permissions, or compliance steps.

4. Onboarding state, milestones, and feature visibility
- Inventory any onboarding status fields, user preferences, checklist state, completion flags, milestones, achievements, feature flags, entitlements, experiments, role/plan gates, UI visibility rules, or server-side authorization rules that affect what new users see.
- Separate feature access control from feature presentation/visibility where possible.
- Identify how state is initialized, updated, persisted, backfilled, tested, and reset.

5. Analytics, observability, and activation measurement
- Inventory product analytics and instrumentation related to signup, account creation, onboarding start/step/complete, first key action, artifact creation, invite acceptance, activation, retention, feature exposure, notifications, and errors.
- Record event names, schemas/types, emitting code paths, destinations, guards, tests, and any dashboards or metric docs in the repo. If metrics/dashboards live outside the repo, mark them unknown.
- Note logging/tracing around onboarding failures, job execution, notification sends, and first-run errors.

6. Lifecycle messaging and return paths
- Map notification systems: email, push, in-app, webhook, CRM, marketing automation, transactional provider, template locations, scheduling/queueing, unsubscribe/consent handling, rate limits, localization, and delivery logging.
- Identify any messages or jobs triggered after signup or onboarding events, without assuming any particular cadence is required.
- Note whether templates include user-, org-, or artifact-specific data and how missing/deleted data is handled.

7. Tests and quality gates
- Inventory relevant unit, integration, end-to-end, contract, analytics, job, and template tests. Note fixtures/factories for new users and onboarding states.
- Identify test gaps as unknowns, not failures, unless code clearly lacks coverage for a material path.

Evidence rules:
- For every confirmed fact, include file path and precise symbol, route, schema/table/column, config key, job name, event name, template, or test name.
- Separate Confirmed Facts, Inferences, and Unknowns. Inferences must state the supporting evidence and uncertainty.
- Do not use production claims, retention rates, delivery rates, or user behavior unless the repository itself contains those data or read-only artifacts.

Deliverable: produce a concise architecture briefing with these sections:
A. System overview and key modules
B. Signup-to-first-session traced flow
C. Domain/core workflow candidates and supporting evidence
D. Onboarding state and feature visibility map
E. Analytics/observability inventory
F. Lifecycle messaging/job inventory
G. Tests and fixtures
H. Material unknowns and repository boundaries
I. Handoff map for the follow-up audit: files/symbols/routes/events/jobs/templates that should be inspected first, plus any runtime evidence that would be needed later.

End your response with: STOP - waiting for the investigation prompt.
investigationPrompt:
You are a read-only repository audit agent. Do not edit files, create branches, implement code, write migrations, change configs, or refactor anything. Use the prior architecture briefing if available, then inspect the repository as needed. Your task is to evaluate a video-derived recommendation as a hypothesis against this repository, preserving uncertainty and separating static evidence from runtime proof.

Hypothesis to evaluate, not assume: for a newly acquired SaaS/product app with strong signup conversion but poor day-seven return, the product should improve activation and early retention through three mechanisms: (1) a guided first-run flow that helps a new user reach the product’s core action within about 60 seconds of signup, using pre-filled templates or smart defaults where appropriate; (2) progressive disclosure that tracks user milestones and reveals more advanced capabilities incrementally rather than showing every feature in the first session; and (3) event-based re-engagement triggers around day one and day seven after signup that reference data the user created or received, rather than generic reminders.

Preserve the speaker’s causal model and qualifications: signup conversion only proves willingness to try, not experienced value; tours, documentation, empty states, and manual setup can delay value; templates/defaults may reduce setup friction; progressive disclosure may reduce overwhelm if readiness is measured reliably; personalized lifecycle prompts may give a concrete reason to return. Also preserve the assumptions: the product has an identifiable core value moment; that moment can occur quickly without required external integration, lengthy manual data entry, compliance review, or human approval; generated/default/demo content can be safe and non-misleading; milestones can represent readiness; feature reveal can be added without harming discoverability; notification permission and delivery channels exist; user-owned data exists to reference; and early churn is materially influenced by onboarding rather than unrelated product, pricing, reliability, missing functionality, product-market fit, or low-intent traffic. Do not strengthen these claims beyond what the repository supports.

Required applicability statuses for each material claim: Confirmed, Partially Applicable, Refuted, Not Applicable, or Needs Runtime Verification. For each status provide exact static repository evidence, missing evidence, assumptions, realistic impact, severity if meaningful, and confidence. When static evidence is mixed but runtime proof is missing, report both facts; do not collapse them into a definitive production conclusion.

Use severity only when useful for prioritization: Critical, High, Medium, Low, or Informational. Base it on actual exposure, frequency, scale, user impact, reliability, exploitability where relevant, and operational cost. Warn against exaggerating a theoretical onboarding concern into a production issue without retention, traffic, or behavioral evidence.

Investigation methodology:

1. Establish the actual new-user lifecycle and core value candidate
- Trace signup/invite/account creation through first authenticated route, onboarding screens, required setup, and first domain workflow. Cite routes, controllers, components, hooks, services, schemas, migrations, config, feature flags, and tests.
- Identify the product’s likely core action or core artifact only from repository evidence such as domain models, primary routes, analytics events, onboarding copy, docs, test scenarios, or naming. If multiple candidates exist, list them and explain uncertainty.
- Check whether the core value moment plausibly can occur in the first session and what must happen first: workspace/org creation, billing/trial setup, integrations, imports, invite acceptance, permissions, verification, approval, data entry, or background jobs.
- Static evidence can show number and nature of required steps, routes, and dependencies. Runtime evidence is required for actual time-to-value, drop-off, latency, error rates, and user comprehension.

2. Evaluate the activation/onboarding-failure premise
- Look for repository-contained metrics definitions or analytics events for signup, onboarding start/completion, core action completion, artifact creation, activation, retention, and day-seven return. Cite exact event names/types and emitters.
- Determine whether the app can measure the claimed funnel and whether events are coherently tied to users/orgs/sessions.
- Do not assert that abandonment is about onboarding unless runtime analytics support it. Note alternative explanations visible in the repo: known bugs, performance hotspots, missing onboarding paths, billing gates, integration failures, empty-state dead ends, unsupported invite states, reliability gaps, or lack of instrumentation. Also list alternatives that cannot be assessed statically, such as traffic quality, pricing, PMF, support quality, and marketing source.
- Applicability question: is the problem diagnosable from current instrumentation, and does static flow evidence make onboarding a plausible contributor?

3. Evaluate the guided first-run and 60-second core-action hypothesis
- Determine whether a guided first-run flow exists. Cite components/routes/services/state fields and how users enter/exit it. Classify it as checklist, wizard, modal tour, documentation links, empty-state guidance, interactive workflow, seeded workspace, import path, or another pattern.
- Check whether the flow leads to creating/completing/receiving the core artifact or workflow before onboarding ends. Cite creation APIs, mutations, services, callbacks, tests, and persistence schemas.
- Inventory templates, sample/demo data, default records, generated content, smart defaults, fixture-based seeding, import helpers, AI generation, or starter configurations. Evaluate whether they are used for real onboarding, only tests/dev, or unrelated examples.
- Check guardrails: labeling sample/demo content, ability to delete/reset, isolation from real data, avoidance of misleading business records, tenant isolation, audit trails, privacy/compliance implications, localization, accessibility, and support for invited users or existing org members.
- Static inspection can estimate friction from required steps and dependencies; it cannot prove completion within 60 seconds. If the repository has E2E timings, performance budgets, synthetic tests, or UX docs, cite them as limited evidence. Otherwise mark the timing claim Needs Runtime Verification.

4. Evaluate tours/documentation/empty-state reliance
- Identify onboarding screens that primarily display static copy, tooltips, product tours, help links, videos, docs, or generic empty states. Cite exact components/templates and linked docs.
- Identify whether these are the main path or supplemental guidance. A docs link is not a failure by itself; determine whether users can still perform the core action directly and whether the UI has actionable next steps.
- Assess impact realistically: harmful only if such mechanisms block or materially delay reaching the core workflow, especially for a meaningful portion of new users. Runtime funnel and session replay/analytics would be needed to prove harm.

5. Evaluate progressive disclosure and milestone-based readiness
- Inventory feature visibility and access logic: feature flags, plan/role entitlements, permissions, experiments, onboarding completion flags, milestone records, user preferences, settings, server-side guards, frontend conditional rendering, navigation items, and empty states.
- Determine whether the app currently exposes broad feature sets immediately, gates features by plan/role only, hides/shows based on onboarding state, or reveals based on demonstrated usage milestones. Cite exact symbols and conditions.
- Check milestone quality if present: event source, idempotency, persistence, backfill, reset behavior, org-vs-user scope, multi-device consistency, race conditions, test coverage, analytics alignment, and whether milestones represent readiness rather than arbitrary session/time counts.
- Check discoverability constraints: power users, admins, invited users, accessibility, search/deep links, support docs, direct URLs, API access, and whether hiding features could break expected workflows or create inconsistent authorization vs visibility.
- Runtime evidence needed: whether progressive disclosure reduces overwhelm, improves activation, or harms conversion for users who need advanced features early. Static evidence can only show whether the mechanism exists and its likely maintenance complexity.

6. Evaluate day-one/day-seven event-based re-engagement
- Inventory lifecycle notifications after signup/onboarding: schedulers, cron jobs, queues, workers, event consumers, marketing automation calls, transactional templates, in-app messages, push notifications, email providers, webhooks, and CRM sync. Cite job names, routes, config keys, templates, and tests.
- Determine trigger basis: fixed time after signup, onboarding incomplete, artifact created/updated, invited to workspace, trial state, inactivity, plan changes, or other events. Specifically check whether day-one and day-seven cadences exist; if different cadences exist, report them without treating them as wrong by default.
- Determine whether messages reference user-owned data or artifacts, and how personalization is generated. Cite template variables, query code, serializers, null handling, fallbacks, deleted/incomplete/stale artifact behavior, permission checks, tenant isolation, and localization.
- Check consent and compliance: unsubscribe/preferences, transactional vs marketing classification, notification permissions, rate limiting, quiet hours, bounce/suppression handling, GDPR/privacy implications, and whether referencing user data in email/push could leak sensitive information.
- Check observability: enqueue logs, send logs, provider responses, retry/dead-letter behavior, idempotency, metrics, dashboards, and tests. Static evidence can show scheduled intent and template content; runtime logs, delivery metrics, open/click/reopen rates, and production configuration are required to prove users receive and respond.

7. Assess current mitigations, constraints, and counterevidence
- Identify existing mitigations that already address the hypothesis: actionable empty states, starter workspace, imported examples, onboarding checklist, contextual nudges, lifecycle campaigns, milestone tracking, analytics, feature flags, or in-app prompts.
- Identify constraints that may make the recommendation unsuitable or only partially suitable: regulated data, B2B admin setup, integration-first value, marketplace/network effects, human approval, customer success onboarding, enterprise SSO/invitations, required billing, long-running imports, or products where showing integrations early is central to value.
- Identify counterevidence: code that already drives users to core workflows; tests ensuring new-user artifact creation; robust instrumentation; personalized notifications already implemented; or absence of any safe user-owned data to reference.
- Do not recommend duplicating mechanisms already present unless evidence shows material gaps.

8. Evaluate solution fit, side effects, operational cost, and safer alternatives
- For guided first-run/default content, assess complexity, data model implications, cleanup/reset burden, support confusion, analytics pollution, tenancy/privacy risks, and test requirements.
- For progressive disclosure, assess maintenance cost, coupling to product milestones, risk of hiding necessary features, role/plan conflicts, QA matrix expansion, and support/documentation burden.
- For re-engagement triggers, assess job infrastructure, deliverability, compliance, personalization failure modes, spam fatigue, localization, monitoring, on-call burden, and incident modes.
- Consider smaller or safer alternatives supported by findings: instrument missing funnel events first; improve core empty state CTA; remove unnecessary setup step; add sample-only sandbox; provide optional template gallery; tune existing lifecycle templates; add fallback-safe personalization; run an experiment; or gather runtime analytics before implementation.

Evidence and reporting requirements:
- Use compact tables where possible. Include a Material Claim Matrix with columns: Claim or assumption; Applicability status; Static evidence with file paths and symbols; Missing/runtime evidence; Impact if true; Severity; Confidence.
- Include a Static vs Runtime Evidence section. Examples of runtime evidence that may be needed here include product analytics funnels, retention cohorts, traces, logs, notification delivery reports, job execution history, session timing, performance metrics, A/B test results, and traffic-source characteristics. Never fabricate these results.
- Include a Causal Chain Assessment: signup -> first authenticated experience -> core action/value moment -> milestone/readiness -> notification reason to return -> day-seven return. Mark each link Supported by Static Evidence, Unsupported, Mixed, or Needs Runtime Verification.
- Include an Existing Mitigations and Counterevidence section.
- Include a Constraints and Side Effects section.
- Include an Areas to Leave Untouched section: code paths that should not be changed because they are unrelated, already adequate, high-risk without product input, or require runtime/business validation first.
- Include Open Questions for product, analytics, operations, privacy/compliance, and customer support.

Final disposition: provide one of Proceed, Modify Recommendation, Reject, or Gather More Evidence. Use Proceed only if static evidence strongly shows absence of these mechanisms, assumptions look valid, and implementation risk is reasonable, while still naming runtime validation needed. Use Modify Recommendation if some mechanisms fit but need scope changes, sequencing, safeguards, or experiments. Use Reject if repository evidence or product constraints contradict the hypothesis. Use Gather More Evidence if retention/activation diagnosis, core value definition, or notification feasibility cannot be established statically.

End with an explicit STOP. No code changes, no implementation plan with code, no commits, no refactors.
